The Hon'ble Apex Court has observed:
".....The object of the interlocutory injunction is to protect the plaintiff against injury by violation of his right for which he could not be adequately compensated in damages recoverable in the action if the uncertainty were resolved in his favour at the trial.

The need for such protection has, however, to be weighed against the corresponding need of the defendant to be protected against injury resulting from his having been prevented from exercising his own legal rights for which he could not be adequately compensated.

The court must weigh need against another and determine where the "balance of convenience" lies' "Prima facie case" means that the Court should be satisfied that there is a serious question to be tried at the hearing, and there is a probability of plaintiff obtaining the relief at the conclusion of the trial on the basis of the material placed before the Court.
"Prima facie case" is a substantial question raised by both sides which needs investigation and a decision on merits.
The Court, at the initial stage, cannot insist upon a full proof case warranting an eventual decree.
When fair question is raised for determination, it should be taken that a prima facie case is established.
The real thing to been seen is that the Plaintiff's claim is not frivolous or vexatious.
The purpose is to preserve status quo until the question before the Court is finally disposed of....."

Hon'ble Supreme Court while explaining the phrase li deceive or cause confusion, relying upon the judgment of privy council in Pianotist Co. Application (1906) 23 RPC 774 has held that:
"For deceptive resemblance two important questions are: (1) who are the persons whom the resemblance must be likely to deceive or confuse and (2) what rules of comparison are to be adopted in judging whether such resemblance exists.

As to confusion, it is perhaps an appropriate description of the state of mind of a customer who, on seeing a mark thinks that it differs from the mark on goods which he has previously bought, but is doubtful whether that impression is not due to imperfect recollection".
12.

Dealing with passing off, in the matter of Laxmikant Vs. Patel AIR 2002 SC 295, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed that it is common in the trade and business to adopt a name, and the courts should protect the goodwill attached to the business name.
An action of passing off will lie wherever the intended name is calculated to deceive or to divert the business from the plaintiff or to cause confusion between the two business.

For deceptive resemblance, the two important questions are who are the persons whom the resemblance must be likely to deceive or confuse, and what rules of comparison are to be adopted, in judging, whether such resemblance exists.

The law of injunction in Intellectual property matter are also intended to remove confusion and deception in the market besides protecting any dilution of the plaintiff's trade goodwill and reputation which has been earned by him legitimately and after hard work and quality products being offered to the consumers.

If the plaintiff is able to show that his legal right is infringed by the defendant or that the product of the defendant is being passed to the consumer as product of the plaintiff, the temporary injunction can and should be granted, in his favour.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
8. The crux of the legal precedents can be seen from the celebrated Gujrat Bottling Co. Ltd. Vs. Coca Cola Company & Ors. [(1996) (16) PTC 89 (SC)], which is the landmark judgment and holds the legal field till date.
The very idea of injunction in Intellectual Property Right's suit is that nobody should be allowed to deceive the actual consumers or try to tread upon the goodwill and reputation created by its proprietor over a period of time to his disadvantage.
An action of passing off will lie wherever the intended name is calculated to deceive or to divert the business from the plaintiff or to cause confusion between the two business.
M/S Nonand Rai Bhola Nath vs M/S Shri Krishna Masala Co on 9 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65621595/
8 13.
The law of injunction in Intellectual property matter are also intended to remove confusion and deception in the market besides protecting any dilution of the plaintiff's trade goodwill and reputation which has been earned by him legitimately and after hard work and quality products being offered to the consumers.
If the plaintiff is able to show that his legal right is infringed by the defendant or that the product of the defendant is being passed to the consumer as product of the plaintiff, the temporary injunction can and should be granted, in his favour.
If the plaintiff is able to prima-facie satisfy the court that its proprietary rights over its trademark/trade name are being infringed by the defendant, to the determent of business interests of the plaintiff,
then a good case is made out for grant of ad- interim injunction protection in its favour.
In terms of Section 28 (1) of Trademarks Act, 1999, the plaintiff has a proprietory right to the MUKESH by MUKESH KUMAR GUPTA exclusive use of the same to the exclusion of others in respect of goods Date:
GUPTA 2024.12.09 18:02:16 -0800 and services for which the Trademark is registered.
The font and style of writing of word "NAV BAHAR/by the defendant on its packaging and labels is quite identical to that of the plaintiff's registered trademark "NAU BAHAR/ .
By virtue of section 29(4) of Trade Marks Act 1999, any use of identical/similar trademarks/labels/logos/trade name by any other party, without permission of registered proprietor, amounts to violation of registered owner's valuable rights and same is not permissible in law.
Thus, the plaintiff has been able to make out a good prima facie case for grant of ad-interim relief.
The balance of convenience also tilts in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant as the plaintiff is a registered Trademark holder and user of the Trademark "NAU BAHAR/ .
Further, it is apparent that the plaintiff would suffer irreparable loss and injury in case the defendant is not restrained from using the trademarks/labels belonging to the plaintiffs.
Having regard to totality of aforenoted reasons, this court is satisfied that plaintiff has been able to satisfy the court on the trinity principle for grant of immediate ad-interim relief to protect its intellectual property rights.
